title: Transactions & Isolation: Writers Colliding
objective: After this lesson you will be able to wrap multi-statement work atomically, name the three classic concurrency anomalies, choose isolation levels (PostgreSQL) and locking modes (SQLite) deliberately, and design retry logic for serialization failures and deadlocks.
why: Single-statement queries are atomic by nature; real work isn't — enroll a developer (insert + update counts + log), transfer anything, migrate data. Concurrent writers interleave, and interleavings produce dirty reads, lost updates, and phantoms unless you choose otherwise. Every 'impossible' data corruption story is this lesson, unlearned.

blocks.text: A **transaction** (`BEGIN … COMMIT`, escape hatch `ROLLBACK`) makes many statements atomic: either all effects persist or none do. The enrollment flow (insert enrollment, bump counters, write audit log) must never half-finish — a crash between statements without a transaction leaves permanent inconsistency no query can detect.

blocks.caption: Transactions turn multi-statement flows into indivisible units

blocks.text: Concurrency bugs have canonical names. **Dirty read**: reading uncommitted data that later rolls back (you acted on rows that never existed). **Non-repeatable read / lost update**: two reads of the same row disagree because a writer committed between them (balances, counters). **Phantom**: a repeated *range* query gains/loses rows as writers insert into the range (reports that don't foot). Every isolation discussion below is about which of these you permit.

rows: Same row differs between your two reads

blocks.text: PostgreSQL offers **READ COMMITTED** (default: no dirty reads, fresh snapshot per statement), **REPEATABLE READ** (snapshot per transaction — no non-repeatables, phantoms possible, serialization errors on write conflicts), and **SERIALIZABLE** (fullest safety; conflicting transactions abort with 40001 — your code *must* retry). SQLite serializes writers with locking instead: one writer at a time, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to reserve the write lock up front (avoiding mid-transaction SQLITE_BUSY), WAL mode for concurrent readers.

blocks.caption: Levels (PG) vs lock reservation (SQLite) — same goal, different machinery

blocks.text: Defaults are sensible starting points (READ COMMITTED / deferred locking); escalate deliberately for money-like invariants (balances, seat counts, enrollment caps) and keep those transactions short — long transactions hold snapshots/locks that starve everyone else. Deadlocks (two transactions locking in opposite order) resolve by always acquiring in the same order plus retry logic, never by hoping.

blocks.title: Retry is part of the code
blocks.text: SERIALIZABLE (and SQLite BUSY) failure modes are *expected control flow*, not bugs: wrap transactions in retry loops with backoff, keep retried units idempotent, and cap attempts. Code that treats serialization errors as crashes will page you at 3am under load — which is exactly when they spike.

Read-modify-write (`read count, +1, write`) loses updates when two writers interleave — each reads 5, writes 6, one increment vanishes. Fixes in ascending strength: single-statement atomic updates (`SET n = n + 1`), optimistic locking (version column + `WHERE version = ?`, retry on zero rows), or SERIALIZABLE. The single-statement form is almost always sufficient and composes with everything.

blocks.query: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id ORDER BY n DESC;
blocks.note: Run this counter snapshot in the sandbox — counters are the data most corrupted by lost updates. Then picture two admins recomputing it concurrently: the reasoning about interleavings starts from numbers you have actually seen.

items: Transactions make multi-statement flows atomic: BEGIN…COMMIT, ROLLBACK on any failure
Three anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable/lost updates, phantoms — each killed by a specific level
PG levels (COMMITTED → REPEATABLE → SERIALIZABLE + retry) vs SQLite locking (IMMEDIATE, short txns, WAL readers)
Lost-update antidote ladder: atomic single statements → optimistic versioning → serializable + retry
Keep transactions short; acquire locks in consistent order; retry loops are production code

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, snapshot per-course enrollment counts (flat GROUP BY). (b) On paper, interleave two writers both doing read-count(5)→insert→write-count(6) on the same course and show the lost increment. (c) For real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write the three fixes: atomic single-statement counter bump, optimistic-version update with retry check, and the SERIALIZABLE transaction with retry pseudocode. State when each is appropriate.
hints: Sandbox snapshot is the practice query — record counts; they are the 'before' photo your interleaving corrupts.
Interleaving: W1 read 5, W2 read 5, W1 write 6, W2 write 6 — two increments, net +1. Draw the timeline; the overlap window is the bug.

Atomic: UPDATE stats SET n = n + 1 WHERE course_id = ? (one statement, no read). Optimistic: UPDATE … SET n = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? + application retry on 0 rows. Serializable: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE … COMMIT with 40001 retry loop.
exercise.solution:
-- (c-i) atomic bump (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
-- UPDATE course_stats SET enrolled = enrolled + 1 WHERE course_id = 5;
-- (c-ii) optimistic: UPDATE course_stats SET enrolled = 6, version = version + 1
--   WHERE course_id = 5 AND version = 3;  -- 0 rows → re-read, retry
-- (c-iii) serializable block with application-level retry-on-40001 loop.
-- Ladder: atomic for counters; optimistic for multi-field edits; serializable for money-like multi-row invariants.
exercise.why: The ladder teaches proportionate response: most counter bugs die at step one, and reaching for SERIALIZABLE everywhere buys latency and retries for safety simple statements already provide. The interleaving sketch is the diagnostic skill — see the overlap window, name the anomaly.

quiz.q: Two writers read count 5, each adds 1, each writes 6. Final count and name?
options: 6 — one increment lost: a lost update (non-repeatable family)
quiz.explain: Read-modify-write interleaves: both base on the same read, one write clobbers the other. Net +1 for two increments — the canonical lost update.

quiz.q: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE transaction aborts with 40001 under load. Correct handling?
options: Log and crash — data is corrupt
Retry the whole transaction (idempotent unit, bounded attempts, backoff) — serialization failures are expected control flow
quiz.explain: Serializable safety is enforced by aborting conflicts; the application contract is retry. Units must be idempotent and bounded — spikes coincide with load, exactly when paging hurts most.

quiz.q: SQLite writer gets SQLITE_BUSY mid-transaction. Best prevention?
options: BEGIN IMMEDIATE to reserve the write lock up front + short transactions + WAL mode for readers
quiz.explain: Deferred locking discovers contention mid-flight; IMMEDIATE fails fast at start instead. Short transactions shrink hold time; WAL lets readers proceed during writes.

quiz.q: Which anomaly does REPEATABLE READ (snapshot per transaction) still permit?
options: Phantoms — new rows matching the range can appear; only SERIALIZABLE's predicate locking kills them
quiz.explain: Snapshots freeze *seen* rows, not range membership. Repeatable reads of the same row are safe; repeated range queries can gain phantoms — the remaining gap SERIALIZABLE closes.

summary: Atomicity via transactions, anomalies named (dirty, non-repeatable/lost, phantom), levels and locks chosen per invariant, retries as production code. Concurrency correctness is designed, never hoped for.
